questions.q: What is the common anti-pattern this lesson describes for fixing "the app can't read this table"?
options: Creating a brand new database for the app
Granting only SELECT on the one specific table needed
Deleting the table entirely
Adding the account to db_owner, which grants full control of the database far beyond the one table that was actually needed
questions.explain: db_owner immediately fixes the symptom but grants far more than needed — the ability to drop tables, change permissions, and read everything — because nobody confirmed the actual specific need.

questions.q: What does the principle of least privilege actually mean, per this lesson?
options: Only the DBA account should ever have any permissions at all
An account starts with no access and gains only the specific permissions it's been shown to need — nothing granted "to be safe"
Permissions should be granted once and never reviewed again
Every account should default to db_owner unless told otherwise
questions.explain: Least privilege is additive and evidence-based: permissions are granted in response to a proven, specific need, not guessed at or granted broadly up front.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the reasons this lesson gives for why the db_owner anti-pattern happens anyway?
options: Time pressure — db_owner fixes the symptom in one line
Azure SQL technically requires db_owner for any application to function
Fear that narrowing access later will break something
Nobody owns the cleanup once the immediate problem is gone
questions.explain: This is false and not something the lesson claims — Azure SQL does not require db_owner for normal application access; time pressure, lack of ownership, and fear of breaking things are the real reasons given.

questions.q: According to this lesson, is least privilege a one-time setup step or an ongoing discipline?
options: A one-time setup step performed only when the database is first created
An ongoing discipline — auditing actual usage, granting additively, and revisiting access as roles change
Something that only applies to server-level logins, never database users
A discipline that applies only during a migration
questions.explain: Least privilege has to be maintained continuously: auditing what's actually used, granting only in response to proven needs, and removing access that's no longer justified.

questions.q: How does DENY (from Lesson 23) let a DBA use a convenient broad role without fully abandoning least privilege?
options: DENY has no relationship to least privilege
DENY automatically converts a role membership into individual grants
DENY cannot be combined with roles at all
DENY can carve out an exception on one sensitive object, overriding the broad role's grant for just that object
questions.explain: A DENY on a specific sensitive table lets you keep a broad, convenient role assignment while still excluding the one object that shouldn't be covered by it.
